input:
Net positive suction head is a crucial consideration in the operation of any pump, and in this worked example we look at how the available net positive suction head, denoted $NPSH_a$, can be determined for a pump that draws water from an open tank. The surface of the water in the tank is exposed to the atmosphere, so the pressure acting on it is the atmospheric pressure of 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, and the difference between these two pressures, which is the pressure available above the vapour pressure, is 81.4 kPa, corresponding to a head of 8.3 m of water. In addition to this, the static lift that the pump has to overcome is 2.7 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.3 m. The available net positive suction head is then given by the following equation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

Substituting the values discussed above into this equation gives an available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ of 5.3 m. It should be noted that the required net positive suction head of the pump at the duty flow is not calculated here but is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin for satisfactory operation.
target:
Determine the available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ for a pump drawing water from an open tank. The tank surface is at atmospheric pressure, $P_{atm}$ = 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure $P_v$ at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift $h_{lift}$ is 2.7 m and the suction-line friction loss $h_f$ is 0.3 m. The available net positive suction head is the head at the pump inlet above the head corresponding to vapour pressure, after the lift and the suction losses are met. The pressure available above vapour pressure is the difference of the two pressures, 81.4 kPa, and division by the weight density $\rho g$ of the water converts that pressure to a head of 8.3 m. Stating the balance in metres of the liquid pumped puts every term in one form: the tank pressure drives the liquid up the suction line, gravity and friction take their share of the head, and what remains is the margin above vapour pressure at the pump inlet. The available net positive suction head is then

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where every symbol is as defined in the set-up above. Thus $NPSH_a$ = 5.3 m, the pressure head less the lift and the friction loss. The pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow is taken from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed it with margin.
